tags: cave, human sacrifice, burning, pre-roman, iron age
description: A cave on the Isle of Skye with a flowing underground stream that appears to have been the focus of ritualised activity over an extensive period of time. the cave has been visited since the Bronze Age at least, but was first deliberately modified around 820-755 BCE. Features like a doorway entrance, external structures like walls and cells, as well as a stairway for easier entrance were created and modified over a nearly 945 year time period. For much of the Iron Age the enclosure at the entrance of the cave appears to have been dominated by large curated hearths, and through out this period there is evidence of offerings of animals, especially pigs, as well as a large amount of human bone, particularly juveniles. In the later Iron Age (probably 185 - 100 BCE) the stairway entrance to the cave was closed off, and after an extended hiatus a inhumation of a woman and two very young children, only one of which appears to have been related to the woman, were interred over the blocked off stairway. Human sacrifice is suggested by the authors, but this is not necessarily convincing.
bibliography: Archaeology, Current. “Subterranean Skye: Exploring the Enduring Significance of High Pasture Cave | The Past,” June 4, 2025. https://the-past.com/feature/subterranean-skye-exploring-the-enduring-significance-of-high-pasture-cave/.
